title: How medicines work in the body
examples: How exactly do painkillers stop the pain message from reaching my brain?
What is the difference between a medicine working on a receptor and blocking a signal?
Can you explain the process scientists use to test if a new drug is safe?

explain.say: Today we learn how medicines interact with your body's systems. We will look at special spots called receptors.

draw.text: How medicines work in the body

explain.say: A receptor is like a lock on your body's cells. Medicines often fit into these locks to cause a change.
Some medicines work by blocking pain signals. They fit into the receptor, stopping the natural signal from getting through.
Scientists test medicines in stages to keep everyone safe. They first test them in test tubes and then in animals.

draw.text: Testing stages: In vitro to clinical

explain.say: A real-life example is when you take an antihistamine for allergies. It blocks receptors that cause you to sneeze or itch.
A common mistake is thinking all medicines work the same way. Some medicines stimulate, while others block signals entirely.

faq.q: Do all medicines have to use receptors to work?
faq.a: No, some medicines work by changing the body's chemistry directly. They might speed up or slow down chemical reactions instead of using a lock.
asks: Do drugs always need a receptor?
What if a medicine doesn't fit a receptor?

faq.q: If a medicine blocks a receptor, does that mean it is bad for the body?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Sometimes blocking a signal is exactly what is needed to treat a condition, like stopping an allergic reaction.
asks: Is blocking a receptor always negative?

faq.q: How long does it take for a medicine to start working after I take it?
faq.a: This depends on the medicine, but generally, it takes time for the drug to travel through your bloodstream and reach the target receptors.

faq.q: What is the difference between a drug and a medicine?
faq.a: A drug is any substance used to treat illness. A medicine is the prepared form of that drug that you take to get better.
asks: Are drugs and medicines the same thing?
What is the difference between the chemical and the pill?

faq.q: Why do scientists need to test medicines in different stages?
faq.a: Testing in stages ensures that the medicine is safe for humans and that it actually works as intended before it reaches the public.
asks: Why are there so many testing phases?
What is the purpose of animal testing?

facts: Receptors are proteins found on the surface of cells.
Some medicines are called agonists because they activate a receptor.
Other medicines are called antagonists because they block a receptor.
Drug testing moves from simple lab tests to complex human trials.

quiz.say: A medicine that fits into a receptor and turns it on is called a/an:
quiz.why: An agonist mimics the body's natural signal, activating the receptor.

wrong.0: This is wrong because receptor is the lock, not the key that turns it.
wrong.2: This is wrong because an antagonist blocks the receptor instead of activating it.
wrong.3: This is wrong because ligand is a general term for any molecule that binds, not the specific action.

quiz.say: If a medicine blocks a pain receptor, what is its primary action?
quiz.why: Blocking the signal prevents the pain message from reaching the correct cell inside the body.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the medicine acts chemically on the surface, not by rebuilding the cell.
wrong.2: This is wrong because stimulating it would likely make the pain signal stronger.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the medicine usually just occupies the receptor temporarily.

quiz.say: Which stage of drug testing involves testing on people?
quiz.why: Human trials are the final, most complex stage to check for safety in people.

wrong.1: This is wrong because test tubes only show basic chemical reactions, not a whole body.
wrong.2: This is wrong because animal models are a step before testing on people.
wrong.3: This is wrong because in vitro means 'in glass' and only refers to lab dishes.
